LASCARS IN THE PARK.
49 Dusky Visitors Who Tried to Call on the King Yesterday.
"PLENTY NO GOOD."
Forty-nine Indian subjects of his Majesty set out from the West India Docks yesterday to pay a ceremonies call at Buckingham Palace.

They were lascars from a steamship which arrived from the East on Saturday. All sailors have a grievance of some kind or other, and these particular men went to lay their special>paint before the King, confident that their woes would be immediately remedied.

They made a picturesque little procession as, led by their two "serangs," or headmen, they passed through Whitechapel. They told the police here and there, "We want see the King." As it chanced the wish was a common one yesterday, but in due course they arrived near to the Palace.

Here the conversation with the police became rather mixed until at last an intelligent constable, realising that they were no mere idle spectators, dispatched them to the India Office with their troubles.
Forty-seven of the forty-nine disposed themselves comfortably upon benches in St. James's Park, and the two serangs were taken before a patient official at the India Office.
The "No Good Ship."

After a lot of broken English it was gathered that their ship was "plenty no good," and that they did not intend to return to her. They had not been discharged, but had just walked off to explain their difficulties to the King.
The India Office agreed to hear their story at a later hour in the day at the Asiatics' Home in Limehouse.
Full of content they trudged back again, Incidentally on the return journey they did see the King, but failed to recognise his Majesty.
Meanwhile, down at the docks a captain and his officers were wondering how a large-sized steamship was to load and get away to Australia in two days with most of her crew absent.

"I can't for the life of me make out what's the matter with them," said the captain. "We heard nothing of this until we reached Cardiff ten days ago. Then they came and explained gravely to me that I was no good; that I made them do too much work, and that the food was bad.

"A day or two later they retracted this, and said the officers were no good. Then they didn't want to go back to Australia; they wanted to go home. Last night a serang came up and said they would go to Australia. This morning they coolly walked off, leaving a month's pay and all their belongings behind. That's the whole story."
Impassive Asiatics.
At the Asiatics' Home later on, where a small and unofficial inquiry was held by the India Office, the lascars gave their version of the affair.

The India Office official attempted to reason. It was not the slightest use. With calm, impressive faces they listened, but declined to return to their ship. They were told that the Asiatics' Home was full, and they could not stop there.

One of the serangs with magnificent mien announced that they would sleep in the streets. As a last resource the penalties of the law were pointed out to them. "You can be sent to prison," said the India Office official severely. The serang serenely replied that he and his brothers would be very willing to go to prison if necessary, but they would not return to the ship.

So in despair the matter was left for the time being. The forty-nine walked solemnly out of the home and sat down in a row on the pavement outside. They endured the gaze of the archins of Limehouse with perfect composure, and when finally ordered off at dusk they sedately marched down the street. Up to a late hour last night they were still hovering about the neighbourhood of the docks.
